{
  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts contain a high density of person entities, specifically judges (often with titles like Dr., Mag., Prof., Hofrat) and litigants (plaintiffs/defendants). The primary challenge is distinguishing between titles and names, and handling complex multi-word names with suffixes or multiple titles. The rules focus on structural patterns of titles followed by capitalized names, and names appearing in specific legal contexts (e.g., 'gegen', 'vertreten durch').",
  "strategy": "Use a combination of title-based patterns for judges/lawyers and context-based patterns for litigants to ensure high precision while capturing the full name span including titles.",
  "note": "Every rule includes output_template and output_key. Patterns use capture groups to isolate the name when necessary, but often match the full title+name string as seen in training examples.",
  "rules": [
    {
      "name": "judge_titles_with_names",
      "description": "Matches judges and officials with their academic/professional titles (Dr., Mag., Prof., Univ.-Prof., Hon.-Prof., etc.) followed by their names.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Senatspräsident(?:in)?(?: des Obersten Gerichtshofs)?|Vizepräsident(?:in)?|Hofrat(?:in)?(?: des Obersten Gerichtshofs)?|fachkundiger Laienrichter(?:in)?|Richter(?:in)?|Schriftführer(?:in)?|Generalprokurator(?:in)?|Anwalt(?:in)?|Rechtsanwalt(?:in)?|Rechtsanwält(?:in)?)\\s+(?:Univ\\.-?Prof\\.\\s+|Hon\\.-?Prof\\.\\s+|Prof\\.\\s+|Dr\\.\\s+|Mag\\.\\s+|Mag\\.\\s+Dr\\.\\s+|DI\\s+|Dipl\\.-?Ing\\.\\s+|Bakk\\.\\s+iur\\.\\s+)?([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "Covers the most common pattern for judges and lawyers in OGH texts where titles precede names. The pattern captures the full title and name string."
    },
    {
      "name": "litigant_names_after_prepositions",
      "description": "Matches names of parties (plaintiffs/defendants) appearing after legal prepositions like 'gegen', 'der klagenden Partei', 'der beklagten Partei'.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:gegen\\s+die\\s+(?:beklagte\\s+)?Partei\\s+|der\\s+(?:beklagten\\s+)?Partei\\s+|der\\s+(?:klagenden\\s+)?Partei\\s+|des\\s+(?:Antragsgegners?|Klägers?|Beklagten?|Antragstellers?)\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Captures party names which often appear without titles in legal contexts. Uses context to disambiguate from other capitalized words."
    },
    {
      "name": "names_after_represented_by",
      "description": "Matches names of lawyers or representatives appearing after 'vertreten durch' (represented by).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:vertreten\\s+durch\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Specifically targets the 'represented by' clause which is a common source of person entities in legal texts."
    },
    {
      "name": "simple_name_at_start_or_after_comma",
      "description": "Matches simple names at the start of a sentence or after a comma, often used for party lists.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:^|[,.])\\s*([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 5,
      "reasoning": "Covers cases where names appear at the beginning of a text or in lists without preceding titles or context markers."
    },
    {
      "name": "names_in_criminal_proceedings",
      "description": "Matches names of accused persons in criminal cases after 'Strafsache gegen' (criminal case against).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Strafsache\\s+gegen\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Specific pattern for criminal proceedings where the accused is explicitly named after 'against'."
    },
    {
      "name": "names_with_multiple_titles",
      "description": "Matches names that have multiple academic titles (e.g., 'Univ.-Prof. Dr.', 'Hon.-Prof. PD Dr.').",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Univ\\.-?Prof\\.\\s+Dr\\.\\s+|Hon\\.-?Prof\\.\\s+PD\\s+Dr\\.\\s+|Hon\\.-?Prof\\.\\s+Dr\\.\\s+|Univ\\.-?Prof\\.\\s+)([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "Handles complex title combinations that are common for senior judges and professors in Austrian legal texts."
    }
  ],
  "deleted_rules": []
}

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation

- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.

- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.

WHAT MAKES A GOOD RULE:
- PRECISION OVER RECALL: A rule that matches 10 things correctly beats one that matches 100 with 20 wrong. Never sacrifice precision for recall. Missing a match is fixable later; a wrong match poisons results.
- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority
